paragraphs: This is my PhD thesis, completed under the supervision of Carlos M MARQUES and defended on 12 September 2017 before Burkhard BECHINGER, Patricia BASSEREAU, Mireille CLAESSENS and Olivier SANDRE.

Cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) are cationic oligopeptides among the most widely studied vectors for the development of targeted drug delivery within the body. Their main applications include, for example, cancer treatment and gene therapy. However, some characteristics of CPPs make their medical use complex, such as their lack of specificity towards target cells and the loss of their cell-penetrating properties when a molecular cargo is grafted onto them. One solution considered to address these issues is to graft CPPs onto self-assembling elastin-like diblock polypeptides (ELPBCs), systems developed by Ashutosh Chilkoti’s team at Duke University (USA). Previous work showed that these macromolecules, known as CPP-ELPBCs, recovered the cell-penetrating properties of CPPs even in the presence of a cargo and also induced specificity towards cancer cells. However, the penetration mechanism of these systems remained unknown. In this thesis, I focused on studying the penetration mechanism of CPPs and CPP-ELPBCs through model lipid membranes, particularly the adsorption of these molecules onto the surface of giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs). The development of a new method for quantifying fluorescence in confocal microscopy allowed me to perform simple peptide-counting measurements at the surface of the vesicles and subsequently carry out thermodynamic measurements of peptide adsorption.
